- When sentiment is high (≥0.6) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is trending up, cap the forecast at 1–2% above recent mean to avoid false momentum.  
- After a strong upward move in price (e.g., >7% from prior day), model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast by 3–5% in next 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is volatile (fluctuating 0.2–0.6) and forecast is trending, apply mean reversion: if forecast deviates >1.5σ from 14-day moving average, adjust toward it.  
- For 30-day horizon, if forecast is consistently >10% above true outcome, reduce by 2–3% per day until convergence with recent 7-day average.  
- When sentiment is rising (e.g., 0.6–0.8) and price is flat or slightly falling, forecast tends to lag — add 1–2% to forecast to catch momentum.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast by 3–5% to avoid sentiment-driven overoptimism.
